content: Sanskrit pronouns change based on person and gender. First person 'Аһаm' (I) and second person 'Tvam' (You) are gender-neutral. Third person pronouns differ: 'Sah' (He), 'Sā' (She), 'Tat' (It).

examples.meaning: He / That male (Third Person Masculine Singular)
She / That female (Third Person Feminine Singular)

content: Sanskrit has three grammatical genders: Masculine (Puṁlliṅga), Feminine Strīliṅga), and Neuter (Napuṁsakaliṅga). Nouns typically end in specific vowels, such as -aḥ for masculine, -ā or -ī for feminine, and -am for neuter in nominative singular.

Verbs are derived from root forms (Dhātus). In Lat Lakāra (Present Tense), third person singular verbs usually end in '-ti' (ति), second person in '-si' (सि), and first person in '-mi' (मि). Subject and verb must agree in person and number.

Sanskrit has 8 cases (Vibhaktis). The Nominative Case (Prathamā Vibhakti) marks the Subject (e.g. रामः - Rama). The Accusative Case (Dvitīyā Vibhakti) marks the Direct Object (e.g. पुस्तकम् - book, रामम् - Rama as object).
